passage: For three weeks, some older boys had been calling me names at the water tap. Then they started hiding my bag and saying I wasn't welcome at the game. I wanted to hit back, but I remembered Miss saying not to. Instead I stayed near Farhan and the other friends at break and stopped going to the tap alone. It didn't stop, so I told Mrs. Sinha. She listened without interrupting. She said, “This is bullying, and it is not your fault.” I cried a bit. It's taking time, but Farhan sits with me and the boys are being spoken to. I am Ganga.

qa.q: Who did Ganga tell about the name-calling?
qa.a: Mrs. Sinha.

qa.q: Why did Ganga not hit back, and what did Ganga do to stay safe?
qa.a: Ganga remembered Miss saying not to hit back, and stayed near Farhan and other friends and stopped going to the tap alone.

qa.q: What did telling Mrs. Sinha change?
qa.a: It gave Ganga a listener who named it bullying, said it was not Ganga's fault and made sure the boys were spoken to.

qa.q: How might Farhan see what happened to Ganga?
qa.a: Farhan probably worries about a friend being targeted and wants to help, which is why sitting with Ganga matters.

grounding: A child recognises repeated taunting and exclusion as bullying, avoids retaliating, stays near safe people and tells a trusted adult.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 6. Jasleen came to me during the break with her hands shaking. For weeks, a small group had mocked her accent, left her out of games and threatened to hide her lunch. She had not hit back and had kept close to two friends. Today she said, “I think this is bullying.” I said yes, that is what repeated taunting and exclusion are, and that being targeted is never her fault. With her agreement, I spoke to Class Teacher Ms. Alka, and we will meet the group's parents. I will see Jasleen twice next week. Counsellor.

qa.q: What did the small group mock about Jasleen?
qa.a: Her accent.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she arrived with shaking hands, and what did she conclude?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and worn down, and she concluded that the repeated taunting, leaving out and threats amount to bullying.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take?
qa.a: The counsellor told Jasleen it is not her fault, spoke to the class teacher with permission and planned to meet the parents and check in again.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's two close friends have felt during these weeks?
qa.a: They may have felt worried and unsure how to help, and their staying close was a real support.

grounding: A child recognises bullying, avoids retaliating, stays with safe people and tells a trusted adult, and adult response follows.

passage: Friday. Bidisha's diary. It happened again on the bus today. Kishore from Class 8 took my water bottle, poured it on my seat and said I'd wet myself, loud enough for everyone. That's four times this week. Monday it was my bag, Tuesday my name, Wednesday he said he'd push me off at my stop. I wanted to throw the bottle at him. I didn't. I moved to the seat behind the driver, where Kishore never sits. Tonight I told Mummy all of it, even the pushing part. She hugged me and said, “This is bullying, and none of it is your fault.” She phoned the class teacher and the bus in-charge straight away. Tomorrow she's taking me to school herself.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha move to on the bus?
qa.a: Bidisha moved to the seat behind the driver.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Kishore poured the water?
qa.a: Bidisha felt humiliated and angry, even wanting to throw the bottle, after a week of taunts and a threat.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do that was wise?
qa.a: Bidisha recognised the pattern as bullying, didn't retaliate, sat near a safe adult and told Mummy everything that night.

qa.q: How did Mummy respond, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She said it was bullying and not Bidisha's fault, and phoned the teacher and bus in-charge straight away, so adults could act.

grounding: Shows a child recognising repeated taunts and a threat as bullying, not retaliating, staying near safe adults and telling a parent.

passage: Every day after school, when Imran walked past the village well, Madhav and his friends were waiting. “Here comes the crow,” they'd say, flapping their arms, and they blocked the path so he had to go the long way through the thorns. Yesterday Madhav said, “Tomorrow we'll throw you in the well.” Imran's hands shook all night. Today he didn't argue or pick up a stone, though he wanted to. He walked home the long way, past Salim Chacha's tea shop, where grown-ups always sat. At home he told his Dada everything, even the well. Dada put down his newspaper. “You did nothing wrong.” That evening, Dada walked to the headmaster's house, and then to Madhav's father.

qa.q: What did Madhav's group say when Imran walked past the well?
qa.a: “Here comes the crow,” flapping their arms.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling after the threat about the well?
qa.a: Imran was frightened, his hands shaking all night after being threatened.

qa.q: Which of Imran's choices kept him safe?
qa.a: He didn't retaliate, walked home past the tea shop where adults sat, and told his Dada everything, including the threat.

qa.q: How did Dada respond to Imran?
qa.a: Dada told him he did nothing wrong and that same evening went to the headmaster's house and to Madhav's father.

grounding: Shows a child recognising daily taunts and a threat as bullying, avoiding retaliation, staying near safe people and telling a trusted adult.

passage: For three weeks at the Johannesburg school, the boys at Bilal's old lunch table had turned their backs whenever he came near. Someone had made a group chat without him and shared a photo of his lunch with laughing faces. Bilal told himself it didn't matter. Then on Monday a message came to his phone: “Don't even think about coming to the match.” Bilal felt sick. He wanted to type something nasty back. Instead he closed the phone and found Zanele, who always sat with the art kids. He sat with them at lunch. When he showed her the message, she said, “That's bullying. Let's show Mr Dlamini.” They went together. Mr Dlamini read it, saved it and called Bilal's parents that afternoon.

qa.q: Who did Bilal and Zanele show the message to?
qa.a: They showed it to Mr Dlamini.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling when the message came?
qa.a: Bilal felt sick and hurt, and tempted to reply with something nasty.

qa.q: What did Bilal do instead of retaliating?
qa.a: He closed the phone, sat near friendly, safe people and, with Zanele, told a trusted teacher the same day.

qa.q: How did Zanele help Bilal?
qa.a: Zanele named it as bullying and went with him to Mr Dlamini, so he didn't have to do it alone.

grounding: Shows a child recognising repeated exclusion and a threat as bullying, not retaliating, staying near safe people and telling a trusted adult.

passage: For the third Saturday running, Sharmila's towel was missing from the bench at the swimming club, and Avni's group sang "Drippy Sharmila" as she stood shivering by the pool. Avni flicked water at her. "Go on, cry." Sharmila's hands curled. She wanted to push Avni straight into the deep end. Instead she breathed out slowly and walked to the lifeguard's chair, where Coach Latha was writing lap times. "Coach, it keeps happening. The towel, the song, every week." Coach Latha put her clipboard down and listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault." Before the session ended, she spoke to Avni's group, found the towel stuffed in a locker, and that evening she rang Sharmila's mother.

qa.q: How many Saturdays in a row had Sharmila's towel gone missing?
qa.a: It was the third Saturday running.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila walk to the lifeguard's chair instead of pushing Avni?
qa.a: She was angry enough to want to push Avni, but she held it in and moved next to a safe adult; she was probably also hurt and tired of the weekly song.

qa.q: How did Coach Latha support Sharmila?
qa.a: She stopped, listened to everything, said it was not Sharmila's fault, and acted the same day: she spoke to the group, found the towel and rang Sharmila's mother.

qa.q: What would change if Sharmila had pushed Avni into the pool?
qa.a: Avni could have been hurt, Sharmila might have been the one blamed, and the repeated taunting could have been hidden behind the push.

grounding: It shows a child recognising repeated taunting as bullying, not hitting back, staying near a safe adult and telling a coach who responds that day.
